entry.title: 4 of the top 10 YouTube channels are AI-generated
entry.summary:
markdown YouTube is quietly sliding into an AI takeover—four of the top 10 channels by subscribers in May now churn out 100% AI-generated videos, from “cute animals in peril” shorts made with Hailuo to ’80s-style synth jams cooked up on Suno. These channels crank out content nonstop (often for just cents a clip), and YouTube’s algorithm can’t get enough: views-to-subscriber ratios have shot through the roof, vaulting AI players from obscurity to tens of millions of followers in mere months.
Meanwhile, YouTube’s doubling down on Shorts—tweaking view counts to favor loops, rolling out Veo-and-Lens AI experiments, and prioritizing quick, clickable clips over costly, human-made productions. As ad dollars flow and creators migrate to TikTok and Instagram, the platform risks becoming a bot circus: soon you might log in and wonder where all the real people went.

entry.title: Sam Altman Slams Meta's AI Talent Poaching Spree: 'Missionaries Will Beat Mercenaries'
entry.summary:
markdown OpenAI CEO Sam Altman fired off a leaked memo slamming Meta’s recent AI talent-poaching binge, warning that “missionaries will beat mercenaries” and predicting “very deep cultural problems” at Facebook’s parent company. He urged researchers to stick with OpenAI—teasing an organization-wide pay review, hyping the upside of OpenAI stock, and touting the startup’s quirky, mission-driven culture as the best place to build AGI “in a good way.”
The memo follows Meta’s announcement of a new superintelligence team led by Alexandr Wang and Nat Friedman, which scooped up several OpenAI researchers. Altman contrasted Meta’s mercenary hiring tactics with OpenAI’s long-term vision and tighter culture, arguing that while other outfits might chase AI for its own sake, OpenAI is all in on safely creating general intelligence—and plans to reward everyone who helps make it happen.

entry.title: Laid-off workers should use AI to manage their emotions, says Xbox exec
entry.summary:
Laid-off Xbox Game Studios producer Matt Turnbull stirred up debate by urging employees affected by Microsoft’s recent wave of 9,100 cuts to lean on AI chatbots like ChatGPT or Copilot for emotional support and job-hunt help. In a now-deleted LinkedIn post, he shared prompt ideas—from crafting tailored resumes and LinkedIn summaries to drafting outreach messages and reframing imposter syndrome—saying these tools can lighten the cognitive load when “mental energy is scarce.”
Turnbull’s advice lands against Microsoft’s $80 billion AI push and a gaming industry already jittery about generative AI’s impact on creativity. While he framed it as practical self-care, many creatives bristled at the notion of using algorithms to process real human emotions, sparking a wider conversation about AI’s role in workplace well-being.

entry.title: A Pro-Russia Disinformation Campaign Is Using Free AI Tools to Fuel a ‘Content Explosion'
entry.summary:
markdown A new report reveals that a Russia-aligned disinformation operation—variously dubbed Operation Overload, Matryoshka, or Storm-1679—has been using free, consumer-grade AI tools since 2023 to churn out a “content explosion.” Between July 2023 and June 2024 they produced 230 unique pieces of fake pictures, videos, QR codes and websites; in the past eight months that shot up to 587. Video output jumped from 150 to 367, most featuring AI-voice cloning or image generation (notably via Flux AI), to push pro-Russian narratives around Ukraine, global elections and immigration.
What’s especially worrying is the campaign’s sheer scale and variety—impersonating media outlets, twisting real experts’ footage, layering multimedia, and going multilingual. The fakes have flooded 600+ Telegram channels and bot armies on X, Bluesky and even TikTok (3 million views before takedowns). Researchers say it marks a shift to faster, more scalable propaganda, leveraging easy-access AI to sow division in democracies worldwide.

entry.title: Cloudflare Just Became an Enemy of All AI Companies
entry.summary:
markdown Cloudflare just flipped the script on generative AI by telling all new customers: “No more free-for-all web scraping.” Starting now, AI bots are blocked by default unless they pay up or get explicit permission—what the company cheekily calls “Content Independence Day.” Big names like Condé Nast, Reddit and Quora are already on board, backing Cloudflare’s push to restore the old traffic-for-content bargain that AI tools have quietly trashed.
But it’s not just a hard stop. Cloudflare plans to roll out a content-value marketplace (think paying for knowledge, not just pageviews) and new protocols so crawlers have to ID themselves and play by the rules. It’s a slick move to protect indie sites from bandwidth-hogging bots, reward original creators, and maybe—just maybe—force AI outfits to start compensating the sources that fuel them.

entry.title: How Much Of Kojima's Games Are Actually Cutscenes? We Did the Maths - IGN
entry.summary:
TL;DR
Crunching the numbers shows Kojima’s cutscene time varies wildly: the original Metal Gear Solid trilogy sits at roughly 20–26 percent cinematics, MGS4 spikes to a hefty 40 percent (hello, 71-minute finale!), then MGS5 drops to just 8 percent. Death Stranding 1 & 2 clock in around 16 percent, a ratio on par with big narrative-driven games like The Last of Us Part II (15.5 percent) or GTA V (12.5 percent). So, too many cutscenes?
It’s era-dependent. Early MGS balanced stealth and story nicely, MGS4 went full-on movie mode, and MGS5 flipped the script with an open world but a lean plot. Death Stranding strikes a sweet spot, blending engrossing gameplay with just enough Kojima-style cinematics. Bottom line: he’s not making movies—but his flair for big-screen storytelling in games is exactly what keeps us hooked.

entry.title: Microsoft has never been good at running game studios, which is a problem when it owns them all
entry.summary:
Microsoft just slashed hundreds of gaming jobs and pulled the plug on headline projects like Rare’s Everwild and The Initiative’s Perfect Dark, part of its fourth round of Xbox layoffs since last year. Cuts also hit Blizzard, Raven Software, Turn 10, King and others, underscoring the messy aftermath of Microsoft’s five-year buying binge—Bethesda, Activision Blizzard and dozens of studios—that ballooned Xbox into the world’s largest publisher but couldn’t keep all those teams humming.
Behind the numbers lies a longer tale: decades of Microsoft mismanaging its studios, from bungled Halo sequels at Bungie and 343 Industries to the rise-and-fall of Lionhead and the identity crisis at Rare. Overcorrecting every leadership hunch—retreating from first-party then overbuying—has left Xbox bloated with big-IP worries and little creative freedom. With next year’s Fable reboot looming, Microsoft’s real challenge is learning to nurture its studios rather than stifle them—or risk more cancellations and layoffs ahead.

entry.title: Anthem's servers are shutting down in January 2026
entry.summary:
EA and BioWare just announced that Anthem will be officially sunset on January 12, 2026. The servers stay up (and the game stays playable) for the next 180+ days, but you can no longer buy premium currency—though you’re free to spend whatever you’ve already got. If you’ve previously purchased the title, you can still download and play it until the shutdown date.
Anthem was built as an online-only experience, so once the servers go dark it won’t work in any capacity. It’ll also be removed from EA Play on August 15, 2025. No BioWare team members were laid off in this process. For the full rundown, check out the FAQ on EA’s site.
